title: The more generic the question, the more generic the interface
description: AI fills the empty spaces with familiar patterns. The more it knows about the real problem, the less it has to make up.

related.title: Clint Intelligence
related.body: In practice: AI inside a CRM, with the designer defining context, limits and criteria.

blocks.text: Something curious is happening with AI design tools.
They're getting really good at producing beautiful interfaces.
Well-organized cards.
Consistent buttons.
Balanced typography.
Convincing dashboards.
Professional-looking landing pages.
And that's exactly why there's a new problem.
A lot of interfaces are starting to look the same.
Aesthetics are no longer enough
When a tool can generate a visually acceptable interface in seconds, aesthetics stop being such a hard advantage to achieve.
The challenge becomes something else:
why should this interface be this way?
That question is still the designer's responsibility.
An AI can create a beautiful dashboard.
But which information should show up first?
It can create an onboarding.
But which step should be cut?
It can create a checkout page.
But which piece of information is blocking conversion?
It can create ten alternatives.
But which one solves the problem best?
AI fills in the empty spaces

data.open: There's a huge number of open decisions.
data.fills: And those assumptions usually come from familiar patterns. That's why you get cards, dashboards, charts, side menus, hero sections, CTA buttons and highlighted metrics.
close: Without those answers, the model has to make assumptions.
But nothing necessarily belongs to that product.

blocks.text: The problem isn't that AI is generic
The tool is doing exactly what it was asked to do.
If the brief is generic, the solution will probably be too.
That's why context has become so important.
The logic is simple:
the more the tool knows about the real problem, the less it has to make up.
Context is part of design
Maybe the prompt is starting to work as a new layer of specification.

data.context: This screen will be used by restaurant operators during peak hours. The user needs to quickly spot new orders, late orders and orders that need intervention. The most important information is the status. The interaction needs to take few clicks. The system already has components for status, filters and tables.
close: The AI has more information to make decisions.
And the designer has more control over the result.

blocks.caption: The same request, with and without context. Context is the raw material of specificity.

blocks.text: Precision starts before the prompt
A designer who doesn't know exactly what they want is unlikely to solve that just by using AI.
The tool can produce more alternatives.
But more alternatives don't necessarily mean more clarity.
Sometimes they just mean more things to review.
That's why there's important work before the prompt:
understanding the problem.
Then:
defining what matters.
Then:
defining what can't happen.
And only then:
asking the AI to explore.
The designer starts working with degrees of freedom
You can let the AI freely explore:
But you can restrict:
Part of the designer's job also becomes deciding:
where the AI can explore and where it shouldn't improvise.
That brings prompting close to a well-known design skill:
working with constraints.
And constraints don't necessarily reduce creativity.
Often, they make creativity more focused.
